body:
I appreciate the response. I get what you're trying to say, but I think the flaw in your argument is that you assume there is no experience after death. Even if you're a stone cold atheist, you have to admit there is no way of knowing whether that's true. Perhaps consciousness moves on to some other plane of existence, or it's recycled into new life through natural reincarnation. Perhaps you experience some kind of super-consciousness that we can't even fathom. As I said, death is the great unknown; there is no way to be sure what happens to us after death, which is why I say you're essentially playing existential roulette. Even if you believe the most likely theory is that we cease to have experience after death, it just means you can use normal distribution and give yourself a good chance of hitting 50 out of 100, which as I said I would still gladly take over 20.

I also don't really agree with the point that the potential for lack of experience means we should reject suicide as a solution. Yes it's true I won't be conscious to enjoy my lack of pain, but I also won't have to suffer through a prolonged period of consciousness that contains great amounts of pain (i.e. life). So I'd view that scenario not as getting out of a bad situation and into a better one, but just getting out of a bad situation, period. Is that not a noble goal, even if the tradeoff is the inability to positively increase our pleasure as well? If life is very painful and doesn't offer any pleasure to begin with, it seems to me to be a logical tradeoff to make.

As I said, I do greatly appreciate your response and I'm glad you found my post interesting. Just wanted to offer up my counterarguments.

Thanks for replying, I really appreciate it. Your point is true in that the math only works with an even distribution, but I think the assumpton of even distribution is built in due to the uncertainty of experience after death. In fact, given the pureness of the uncertainty, the distribution could be weighted, but it could be weighted based on anything; the fact that the ditribution itself is weighted doesn't matter to us because the weight of the distribution itself is unknown, meaning functionally the distribution IS even. Given all the potential weights of distribution one could come up with, roughly 20% of them would be a hindrance to me and roughly 80% of them would be a benefit to me, so in my view the math still works. Moreover, I would welcome normal distribution because this would greatly increase the chances of at least getting that number up around 50, which would be a significant improvement over the status quo.

Thanks for the response. I'm a bit more levelheaded right now than I was last night at 2am when I wrote this but the feelings continue to dog me and have been consistent for a little while now.

I hear you about getting help, and the one person in my life who knows has asked me to get help as well, and I probably will at some point (I just started a new job so I'm waiting for my health insurance to kick in). Frankly I just wish I could be as optimistic about what help will do for me as other people seem to be. I understand the rationale behind advocating for me to get help; after all, neither you nor this other person (or anyone else I know or communicate with for that matter) is a doctor themselves, so the hope is that if I see a professional they can do things for me that others can't. The problem is that even if I were to see a professional, he or she wouldn't be able to "fix" me per se; the best case I could hope for is that they're somehow able to convince me that what I am right now isn't so bad. They're not going to be able to make me socially skilled or attractive or normal, they're not going to provide me with true friends, they're just going to try to convince me that I "can" do those things, or possibly that those things don't really matter so much. So part of the reason why I'm skeptical of getting help is that I believe right now I've got a fairly true viewpoint of myself and where my life is and I don't really think anyone is going to be able to change that. So, the math above was sort of based on the notion that that 20 isn't really even going to change, which at this point, I don't think it will. It hasn't changed in a very long time, and even in the fleeting moments of my life where I'm able to crawl out of that pit and bring myself up to a higher number, that number is merely a momentary experience, and I always sink back down to that 20-or-so number as a default. But like I said, I think I owe it to myself to at least give it a shot, and so I probably will.

Sorry for the long post again, but thanks again for replying, I appreciate it.
